questions.question: What is an AMI and why would you use it?
questions.answer: An AMI (Amazon Machine Image) is a pre-configured template that contains everything needed to launch an EC2 instance: operating system, applications, files, and configuration settings. You use AMIs to launch servers quickly and consistently. Instead of manually installing and configuring software on every new server (which takes hours), you configure one server perfectly, save it as an AMI, and launch unlimited identical servers from that template in minutes. This ensures consistency, speeds up deployment, enables rapid scaling, and supports disaster recovery.

questions.question: Explain the five types of AMIs and when you would use each.
questions.answer: There are five AMI types: (1) Official AWS AMIs - created by AWS, highest trust, regular updates - use for production workloads (Amazon Linux 2023, Ubuntu Server). (2) Marketplace AMIs - from verified vendors with pre-installed software - use when you need commercial software without manual installation (MongoDB, SAP). (3) Third-party AMIs - from external vendors - use when you have established vendor relationships. (4) Community AMIs - unverified public AMIs - NEVER use for production, only personal learning. (5) Custom AMIs - created by you - use for standardized deployments with your specific configuration. For production, stick with Official or Custom AMIs.

questions.question: What's the difference between an AMI and an EC2 instance?
questions.answer: An AMI is a static template or blueprint, while an EC2 instance is a live, running virtual server. The relationship is like a house blueprint versus actual houses: one AMI can create unlimited instances. The AMI is unchanging and just defines what software is installed. The instance is dynamic, running processes, consuming resources, and costing money per hour. You can also reverse the process - take a running instance, customize it, and create a new AMI from it for future deployments.

questions.question: Why does Linux dominate cloud computing?
questions.answer: Linux dominates cloud computing (approximately 70% of EC2 instances) for several key reasons: (1) Zero licensing costs - no Windows Server fees when running hundreds of instances saves thousands of dollars. (2) Lower resource requirements - Linux needs less RAM and CPU, meaning smaller, cheaper instance types. (3) Superior automation - command-line tools make scripting and Infrastructure as Code easier. (4) Native container support - Docker and Kubernetes were built for Linux. (5) Stability and security - Linux servers run for months without reboots. (6) Customization - you can modify anything in the OS. For these reasons, most web servers, databases, and cloud-native applications run on Linux.

questions.question: Explain the Linux system architecture layers.
questions.answer: Linux operates as six layers: (1) Hardware - physical or virtual compute resources (CPU, RAM, disk). (2) Linux Kernel - core OS managing resources, process scheduling, memory, device drivers. (3) System Libraries - reusable code modules like glibc providing common functions. (4) GNU Utilities - command-line tools like ls, grep, awk for system operations. (5) Shell - command interpreter (bash, zsh) that takes user commands and calls kernel functions. (6) User Applications - the actual programs you run (web servers, databases, custom apps). Each layer builds on the one below, with applications never directly accessing hardware - everything goes through the kernel for security and portability.

questions.question: What is the role of the Linux kernel?
questions.answer: The Linux kernel is the core of the operating system that directly manages all hardware resources. Its key responsibilities include: Process Management (scheduling which programs get CPU time), Memory Management (allocating RAM to applications, handling virtual memory), Device Drivers (interfacing with hardware like disk and network), File System (managing files and directories), Network Stack (TCP/IP implementation), and Security (access control, user authentication). In EC2, the kernel interfaces with virtualized hardware provided by AWS's hypervisor. Understanding the kernel is crucial for performance troubleshooting because it controls resource allocation.

questions.question: Why is command-line interface (CLI) preferred over GUI in cloud computing?
questions.answer: CLI is preferred in cloud computing because it enables automation, which is impossible with graphical interfaces. You can write scripts to manage hundreds or thousands of servers simultaneously - imagine clicking through GUI menus 1000 times versus running one script across 1000 servers. CLI enables Infrastructure as Code (defining infrastructure in text files), CI/CD pipelines (automated deployments), configuration management (Ansible, Chef), and remote management via SSH with minimal bandwidth. All modern DevOps practices rely on CLI. While GUI is easier for beginners, CLI is essential for professional cloud operations at scale.

questions.question: Explain Security Groups and their key characteristic.
questions.answer: Security Groups are virtual firewalls that control inbound and outbound network traffic to EC2 instances. Their key characteristic is that they're stateful - if you allow inbound traffic, the response traffic is automatically allowed outbound without needing separate rules. For example, if you allow inbound SSH on port 22 from your IP address, when you connect, the return traffic automatically flows back without needing an outbound rule. This differs from stateless firewalls where you'd need separate inbound and outbound rules. Security Groups are instance-level protection and are a fundamental security control in AWS.

questions.question: What happens to your data when you stop versus terminate an EC2 instance?
questions.answer: When you STOP an instance: EBS volumes remain attached and all data is preserved. You stop paying for compute (CPU, RAM) but continue paying for EBS storage, which is much cheaper - typically 70-90% cost savings. The instance can be restarted later with all data intact. When you TERMINATE an instance: by default, the root EBS volume is deleted and all data is lost permanently. The instance cannot be restarted. However, you can configure EBS volumes to persist even after termination by disabling the 'delete-on-termination' flag. The key difference: STOP preserves everything and saves money, TERMINATE deletes everything and eliminates all charges.

questions.question: What are Key Pairs and why are they critical?
questions.answer: Key Pairs are cryptographic public-private key pairs used for SSH authentication to Linux instances. The public key is placed on your EC2 instance (like a padlock), and you keep the private key (.pem file) securely on your computer (like the key). When you connect via SSH, your private key proves you're authorized to access the instance. Key Pairs are critical because: (1) They're the ONLY way to access Linux instances initially - there's no password. (2) If you lose your private key, you permanently lose access to the instance with no recovery possible. (3) They're more secure than passwords. Always back up your private key files securely and never share them.

questions.question: Describe a time when you had to choose between different AMI types for a project.
questions.answer: (Situation) I was setting up infrastructure for a new web application that needed to run on Linux with Node.js, MongoDB, and custom monitoring tools. (Task) I needed to decide between using an Official AMI, Marketplace AMI, or creating a Custom AMI. (Action) I evaluated the options: Marketplace had pre-configured MongoDB but included licensing costs and components we didn't need. Community AMIs were ruled out due to security risks. I chose to start with an Official Amazon Linux 2023 AMI, installed and configured Node.js, MongoDB client tools, and our monitoring agents, then created a Custom AMI named 'WebApp-Prod-v1.0'. (Result) This Custom AMI enabled us to launch 15 production servers in under 10 minutes with perfect consistency, and we later used it to rapidly scale during a traffic spike.

questions.question: Walk me through how you would create and deploy a custom AMI.
questions.answer: (Situation) My team needed to standardize our production web server configuration across 50+ instances. (Task) Create a custom AMI that includes all required software and configurations. (Action) Step 1: Launched an EC2 instance from Amazon Linux 2023 Official AMI. Step 2: Connected via SSH and installed required software - Nginx web server, SSL certificates, monitoring agents, security hardening configurations. Step 3: Tested all functionality thoroughly. Step 4: Stopped the instance for consistency. Step 5: Right-clicked instance in AWS Console → Image → Create Image, named it 'WebServer-Production-v1.0-20251006' with detailed description. Step 6: Waited 10 minutes for AMI creation. Step 7: Launched test instance from new AMI, verified all software was pre-installed and working. (Result) Successfully deployed the custom AMI to production, reducing new server setup time from 2 hours to 5 minutes and eliminating configuration inconsistencies.

questions.question: Describe a situation where understanding Linux architecture helped you troubleshoot an issue.
questions.answer: (Situation) Production web server was experiencing slow response times despite seemingly adequate resources (CPU and RAM not maxed out). (Task) Identify and resolve the performance bottleneck within 1 hour to meet SLA. (Action) Understanding Linux layered architecture, I checked each layer: Started with top command showing normal CPU usage. Checked memory with 'free -m' - found high buffer/cache usage but plenty of free memory. Used 'iostat' to check disk I/O - discovered disk wait times were extremely high. Realized the kernel was bottlenecked on slow disk I/O, not CPU. Checked EBS volume type - it was using old magnetic storage. Upgraded to gp3 SSD volumes which provide consistent performance. (Result) Response times improved by 300%, resolved within 45 minutes. This demonstrated that understanding kernel resource management (I/O scheduling) was essential to identifying that the bottleneck was disk, not compute.

questions.question: How would you handle a situation where you lost the private key for a critical production instance?
questions.answer: (Situation) The only developer with access to production database server's private key left the company suddenly, and the key wasn't backed up. We needed access to apply critical security patches. (Task) Regain access to the instance without the original key while maintaining data integrity. (Action) Since direct SSH without the key is impossible, I used AWS Systems Manager Session Manager which provides browser-based shell access without SSH keys (if the SSM agent was pre-installed, which it was on our Amazon Linux instances). Alternatively, if SSM wasn't available, I would: (1) Stop the instance, (2) Detach the root EBS volume, (3) Attach it to a temporary instance as a secondary volume, (4) Mount the volume and modify ~/.ssh/authorized_keys to add a new public key, (5) Reattach to original instance and restart. (Result) Regained access within 30 minutes using Session Manager, immediately created and securely backed up new key pairs, documented the procedure, and implemented policy requiring key backup in password manager.

questions.question: Explain how you would design an AMI versioning strategy for a team deploying updates weekly.
questions.answer: (Situation) Fast-paced development team deploying application updates every week needed a way to track AMI versions and enable quick rollbacks. (Task) Design a sustainable AMI versioning and lifecycle strategy. (Action) Implemented the following strategy: Naming Convention - [Application]-[Environment]-[Version]-[Date] (e.g., WebServer-Prod-v2.3-20251006). Version Increments - Minor version for patches/small updates (v2.3 → v2.4), major version for significant changes (v2.9 → v3.0). AMI Creation - Create new AMI after each successful deployment and testing cycle. Retention Policy - Keep last 5 versions for production, last 3 for staging, last 2 for development. Monthly cleanup of AMIs older than 6 months. Tags - Environment=Production, Version=2.3, CreatedBy=CI-CD-Pipeline, Date=2025-10-06. (Result) This provided clear version history, enabled instant rollback to any of last 5 versions, reduced AMI storage costs by 60% through cleanup, and integrated seamlessly with CI/CD pipeline.

questions.question: How would you troubleshoot an EC2 instance that won't accept SSH connections?
questions.answer: (Situation) Production web server suddenly became inaccessible via SSH, affecting team's ability to deploy updates. (Task) Diagnose and fix SSH connectivity issue using systematic troubleshooting. (Action) Followed methodical approach: (1) Checked instance status - confirmed instance is 'running' in AWS Console, both status checks passing. (2) Verified Security Group rules - found SSH port 22 was accidentally removed during recent security audit. Added rule allowing SSH from my IP. (3) Confirmed network routing - VPC had internet gateway, route table correct, instance in public subnet with public IP. (4) Tested with 'ssh -vvv' for verbose output - connection now succeeding. (5) If that hadn't worked, would check: key permissions (chmod 400), correct username (ec2-user vs ubuntu), NACL rules, OS-level firewall (iptables). (Result) Restored SSH access in 10 minutes, documented proper Security Group configuration, implemented Infrastructure as Code to prevent future accidental changes.

questions.question: Describe how you would implement Infrastructure as Code using AMIs.
questions.answer: (Situation) Manual infrastructure deployment was causing inconsistencies and taking 2+ hours per environment. (Task) Implement Infrastructure as Code using AMIs and automation tools. (Action) Designed the following workflow: (1) Packer - Used HashiCorp Packer to automate AMI creation from code. Configuration files define: base AMI, shell scripts for software installation, provisioners for configuration management. (2) Terraform - Created Terraform modules to launch instances from AMIs, defining instance types, security groups, networking. (3) CI/CD Pipeline - GitHub commit triggers Jenkins pipeline: runs Packer to build new AMI, tags AMI with version and git commit hash, runs Terraform to deploy instances from new AMI, executes automated tests. (4) Version Control - All configurations stored in Git with semantic versioning. (Result) Reduced deployment time from 2 hours to 15 minutes, achieved perfect consistency across environments, enabled atomic rollbacks, eliminated manual configuration errors, and created auditable infrastructure history.

questions.question: How would you design a multi-region deployment strategy using AMIs?
questions.answer: (Situation) Global application needed to serve users from multiple continents with low latency. (Task) Design multi-region deployment strategy ensuring consistency across regions. (Action) Implemented the following architecture: (1) Golden AMI Creation - Created 'golden' AMI in primary region (us-east-1) with all application code, configurations, dependencies. (2) AMI Replication - Automated AMI copying to secondary regions (eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1) using AWS CLI and Lambda function triggered on new AMI creation. (3) Regional Customization - Each region's AMI had region-specific configurations (time zones, regional API endpoints) via user data scripts. (4) Version Synchronization - Maintained same AMI version numbers across regions, deployment automation ensured all regions updated simultaneously. (5) Testing - Deployed to one region first, ran automated tests, then propagated to remaining regions. (Result) Achieved consistent global deployments, reduced latency for international users by 70%, enabled region-level disaster recovery, and maintained deployment consistency with centralized golden AMI.

questions.question: Explain how you would use AMIs for disaster recovery.
questions.answer: (Situation) Company required 4-hour Recovery Time Objective (RTO) for critical applications. (Task) Design disaster recovery strategy using AMIs to meet RTO requirement. (Action) Implemented layered DR approach: (1) Scheduled AMI Creation - Created AMIs of all production servers every 24 hours via Lambda function, tagged with backup date. (2) Cross-Region Backup - Automatically copied AMIs to DR region (if primary is us-east-1, backup to us-west-2). (3) Infrastructure as Code - Maintained Terraform templates for entire environment, tested quarterly by deploying in DR region. (4) Data Backup - EBS snapshots of all volumes every 6 hours, replicated to DR region. (5) Recovery Procedure - Documented: launch instances from latest AMI, attach restored EBS volumes, update DNS to DR region. Runbook tested quarterly. (6) RPO/RTO Calculation - Recovery Point Objective 6 hours (snapshot frequency), Recovery Time Objective 30 minutes (AMI-based launch time). (Result) Achieved sub-1-hour recovery time (exceeding 4-hour requirement), successfully tested quarterly DR drills, maintained compliance requirements.

questions.question: How would you optimize costs when using multiple AMIs?
questions.answer: (Situation) Team had created 50+ AMIs over time, incurring unnecessary storage costs. (Task) Reduce AMI storage costs while maintaining necessary backups. (Action) Implemented AMI lifecycle management: (1) Audit - Inventoried all AMIs, identified 30 AMIs older than 6 months not used in last 90 days. (2) Retention Policy - Production: keep last 5 versions plus monthly snapshots for 1 year. Staging/Dev: keep last 3 versions. (3) Automated Cleanup - Created Lambda function running weekly: deregister AMIs matching deletion criteria, delete associated snapshots, send report of deleted AMIs. (4) Tagging Strategy - Required tags: Environment, Application, CreatedDate, LastUsed, allowing automated identification of candidates for deletion. (5) Cost Analysis - Each AMI's snapshots averaged 15GB = $0.05/GB/month = $0.75/month × 30 unused AMIs = $22.50/month saved. (Result) Reduced AMI storage costs by 65%, maintained necessary backups, created sustainable lifecycle management, documented retention policies.

questions.question: Design a highly available architecture using AMIs and explain your design decisions.
questions.answer: For a highly available e-commerce application, I would design: (1) Multi-AZ Architecture - Deploy instances across 3 Availability Zones in one region, using Application Load Balancer for traffic distribution. (2) AMI Strategy - Create separate AMIs for each tier: web-server AMI (nginx, application code), app-server AMI (business logic), cache-server AMI (Redis). Each tier can scale and update independently. (3) Auto Scaling - Configure Auto Scaling Groups using custom AMIs, minimum 6 instances (2 per AZ), scale up to 30 based on CPU and request count metrics. (4) Blue-Green Deployment - Create new AMI version, launch new Auto Scaling Group (green), test, shift traffic from old (blue) to new, maintain blue for quick rollback. (5) Database Layer - Use RDS Multi-AZ for automatic failover, separate from compute AMIs. (6) Monitoring - CloudWatch alarms on instance health, Auto Scaling automatically replaces failed instances from AMI. This design provides 99.95% availability, handles AZ failures automatically, enables zero-downtime deployments, and supports rapid scaling during traffic spikes.

questions.question: How would you implement immutable infrastructure using AMIs in a CI/CD pipeline?
questions.answer: Immutable infrastructure means never modifying running servers - instead, create new instances with updates. Implementation: (1) Development - Developers commit code to Git. (2) Build Phase - CI pipeline (Jenkins/GitLab) triggers: builds application, runs unit tests, creates Docker container if containerized. (3) AMI Baking - Packer builds AMI: starts from base Amazon Linux 2023, installs application code, configures system settings, hardens security, creates versioned AMI (AppServer-v2.5.3-commit-abc123). (4) Testing Phase - Launches test instances from new AMI, runs integration tests, security scans, performance tests. If tests fail, AMI is deleted. (5) Deployment Phase - Terraform updates Auto Scaling Group launch template to new AMI, Auto Scaling performs rolling replacement: launches new instances, waits for health checks, terminates old instances. (6) Rollback - If issues detected, Terraform reverts to previous AMI version instantly. Benefits: No configuration drift (servers never modified), atomic rollbacks, traceable history (every AMI tied to git commit), simplified security (replace instances rather than patch), and consistent environments.

questions.question: Explain how you would design an AMI sharing strategy for a multi-account AWS organization.
questions.answer: For an organization with separate AWS accounts for development, staging, and production: (1) Centralized AMI Account - Create dedicated 'AMI Factory' AWS account where all golden AMIs are built and maintained. This ensures single source of truth. (2) AMI Build Pipeline - Automated Packer pipeline in AMI Factory account: builds AMIs from standardized configurations, runs security scanning (Inspector, Vulnerability scans), tags AMIs with version, compliance status, approved-for tags. (3) Cross-Account Sharing - Use AMI permissions to share approved AMIs with specific account IDs: development accounts get dev-approved AMIs, production accounts only get production-certified AMIs after full testing. (4) Compliance Scanning - Only AMIs meeting CIS benchmarks and passing security scans are tagged 'production-approved' and shared with production accounts. (5) Service Control Policies - Use SCPs to prevent production accounts from launching instances from non-approved AMIs. (6) Versioning - Semantic versioning across organization, centralized change log. Benefits: Centralized control, standardization across accounts, compliance enforcement, reduced duplication, and clear approval workflow.

questions.question: How would you migrate from configuration management (Chef/Ansible) to an AMI-based deployment model?
questions.answer: Migration strategy from mutable to immutable infrastructure: (1) Assessment Phase - Inventory current Chef/Ansible configurations, identify static components (rarely change) vs dynamic (change frequently). Static components are best for AMIs, dynamic for runtime configuration. (2) Hybrid Approach - Don't migrate everything at once. Phase 1: Bake common components into AMI (OS hardening, monitoring agents, common libraries). Phase 2: Use user data scripts for instance-specific configuration (environment variables, region-specific settings). Phase 3: Gradually move more configuration into AMI as team gains confidence. (3) AMI Build Pipeline - Convert Chef cookbooks/Ansible playbooks to Packer provisioners, maintain git repository of AMI build configurations. (4) Testing Strategy - Deploy AMI-based instances alongside existing Chef-managed instances, compare configurations, run parallel testing. (5) Cutover - Blue-green deployment: launch new AMI-based Auto Scaling Group, shift traffic, maintain rollback capability for 2 weeks. (6) Benefits Realized - Faster deployment (no configuration runs on boot), more reliable (baked-in configuration), easier rollback (entire server state in AMI), simplified infrastructure (less configuration management infrastructure). Challenges: Larger AMI storage costs, slower iteration during development (AMI rebuild vs configuration change).

questions.question: Design a comprehensive AMI security hardening and compliance strategy.
questions.answer: Comprehensive security strategy for AMI management: (1) Baseline Security AMI - Create organizational base AMI: CIS benchmark compliance, remove unnecessary packages, configure SELinux/AppArmor, disable unused services, set up centralized logging, install security agents (GuardDuty, Inspector). (2) Build-Time Security - Automated scanning in AMI build pipeline: Vulnerability scanning (scan for CVEs), Configuration validation (ensure hardening applied), Malware scanning, Secrets detection (prevent hardcoded credentials), License compliance checking. Only AMIs passing all scans proceed to production. (3) Access Control - Encrypt all AMIs with KMS, restrict AMI launch permissions to specific IAM roles, use Service Control Policies to prevent launching non-compliant AMIs, implement least-privilege IAM for AMI management. (4) Patching Strategy - Monthly security AMI releases with latest patches, automated notifications to teams when new security AMI available, 30-day deadline for teams to migrate to latest AMI. (5) Audit and Compliance - Tag all AMIs with security compliance metadata, use AWS Config rules to detect non-compliant instances, automated monthly reports on AMI compliance status, retention of security scan results for audit. (6) Incident Response - Process to rapidly create and deploy emergency security AMIs within 4 hours for critical vulnerabilities. This ensures all infrastructure meets security standards, provides audit trails, enables rapid response to vulnerabilities, and maintains compliance with regulatory requirements.
